title: A novel mechanism for spontaneous ExB shear layer formation in scrape-off-layer plasmas
abstract: We present a novel mechanism for spontaneous shear-flow generation in the scrape-off layer (SOL) of magnetically confined plasmas, arising at abrupt changes in the sheath connection length . Such transitions occur naturally in the Wendelstein 7-X stellarator. Applying a critical balance treatment for interchange turbulence, we find that sets the equilibrium pressure gradient and hence the radial electric field away from the transition, producing an shear around the transition comparable to the turbulence growth rate. High-fidelity simulations are shown to be consistent with the theoretical prediction.

title: Evolution of Jeans instability in nonthermal magnetized complex plasmas
abstract: The classical Jeans instability framework provides a conceptual foundation for understanding self-gravitational collapse and subsequent star formation in interstellar environments. However, cosmic plasmas are inherently magnetized and frequently collisionless, exhibiting significant departures from local thermodynamic equilibrium. While linear theories predict initial instability thresholds, they fail to track the long-term nonlinear runaway dynamics. We present a fluid simulation investigating the nonlinear evolution of the Jeans instability in a magnetized tricomponent complex (dusty) plasma. The constituent nonthermal electrons and ions are governed by the -distribution law, while the heavier dust grains are treated in a fluid framework, coupled with a uniform ambient magnetic field. The numerical architecture utilizes a fourth-order finite difference method (FDM) for spatial gradients and a second-order leap-frog time-integration scheme. We systematically investigate the complex interplay among the self-gravitational attraction, nonthermal electrostatic screening, and magnetic pressure across a wide range of magnetic field strengths and degrees of nonthermality. It is found that enhanced nonthermality accelerates structural localization, while the magnetic field introduces a critical pressure barrier that suppresses the instability. In highly magnetized environments, thermal and nonthermal systems exhibit identical growth rate characteristics, indicating that magnetic pressure dominates the nonthermal thermostatistics in the strong magnetic regime. This study develops a comprehensive and numerically robust framework to understand early-stage star formation and evolution processes in nonthermal astrophysical media.

title: Plasma transport by carrier electrons: classical coefficients across ionization and magnetization
abstract: The classical transport of magnetic field and electron energy in a plasma requires the use of coefficients that depend on plasma ionization and magnetization . This paper explains these scalings through studying the electron velocities responsible for each transport process. Both electron-electron collisions and magnetization affect higher velocity electron populations preferentially, lowering the carrier velocities; transport carried by a high energy electron population is therefore more suppressed by both electron-electron collisions and magnetization than transport carried by lower velocities. Carrier Hall parameters are defined for each coefficient such that magnetization can be described independent of ionization. An analytic idealized coefficient with a single rigid carrier velocity reproduces many of the characteristics of the coefficients, in particular thermal conductivity, but overestimates plasma magnetization due to magnetization itself lowering the carrier velocity. A single moving carrier model improves agreement, but cannot describe the smoothness of the Righi-Leduc coefficient, which originates from being an average over a range of carrier velocities. This is the first paper in a 3-part series; the subsequent papers will extend the carrier picture to non-local heat-flux (paper 2) and non-local magnetic field evolution (paper 3).

title: Exact nonsymmetric vacuum magnetic field with nested toroidal flux surfaces and nonzero rotational transform
abstract: We show that an exact vacuum magnetic field without continuous Euclidean symmetry can fill a bounded solid torus with nested toroidal flux surfaces and nonzero rotational transform. We construct such a field in closed form and show that it is nowhere vanishing. Every off-axis field line closes after one toroidal transit and one poloidal turn, with rotational transform on every flux surface. The solution provides an exact benchmark for three-dimensional equilibrium codes.

title: Kinetic Fluctuation-Dissipation Relation in collisionless plasmas: a correlated noise source
abstract: We here focus on small-scale dynamics of collisionless plasmas by employing a generalized kinetic Langevin framework driven by a stochastic time-correlated forcing. Our investigation captures the steady-state Fluctuation-Dissipation Relation (FDR) where the energy injection at low frequencies is due to the time-correlated forcing and the small-scale energy conversion occurs via Landau damping, the latter --though formally reversible-- acting as an effective dissipation mechanism. We analytically extract the resulting asymptotic spectral scalings across multiple physical regimes and characterize the velocity-space cascade by decomposing the plasma distribution function with Hermite polynomials. The framework is then generalized to a multi-scale forcing scenario in which correlation rates are distributed according to a power-law distribution. This extension provides closed-form analytical expressions that may serve to interpret spacecraft in-situ observations. All analytical predictions are successfully validated through direct numerical integrations of the underlying kinetic equations.

title: Exact Nonsymmetric Vacuum Magnetic Fields with Nested Toroidal Surfaces
abstract: We give a constructive method for exact vacuum magnetic fields whose lines fill nested toroidal surfaces in ordinary space, without continuous spatial symmetry. Complex potential theory on an algebraic curve, combined with doubly periodic traveling waves from soliton theory, gives closed forms for the field, its potential and a surface label. Free parameters set the rotational transform and the magnetic shear, including exactly constant irrational transform. The same fields are exact potential flows with toroidal stream surfaces, and give stringent tests for standard stellarator codes.

title: Exponential Growth of Turbulent Cross Helicity in Shear-Flow-Driven Turbulence
abstract: Cross helicity, the velocity--magnetic-field correlation, is an ideal invariant of incompressible magnetohydrodynamics and constrains energy cascades and magnetic-field generation. Although cross helicity typically decays via visco-resistive effects, we analytically demonstrate that it grows exponentially in sheared inhomogeneous turbulence. This cross-helical shear instability is confirmed using three-dimensional numerical simulations. Growth requires a nonzero gradient of the Reynolds--Maxwell stress to produce turbulent cross helicity; this production overcomes effective losses when shear exceeds a threshold set by the ratio of turbulent magnetic to momentum diffusivities.

title: Rapid Variability of Radiative Signatures from Driven Relativistic Reconnection
abstract: Rapid variability in energetic flares is a distinctive feature of high-energy emission from many magnetically dominated astrophysical sources. We investigate the radiative variability of driven relativistic magnetic reconnection using Particle-in-Cell simulations of strongly magnetized flux tubes pushed to merge at driving speed . This setup captures the onset of reconnection and provides a controlled model for single reconnection-driven flares near compact objects, where magnetic structures can be twisted, sheared, and forced to merge by turbulent accretion flows or relativistic frame dragging. We find that the merger efficiently accelerates particles into nonthermal distributions, producing synchrotron emission whose variability tracks the reconnection phases. We identify two regimes: a quasi-steady, weakly driven regime for , and strongly driven regime for . The transition occurs when the driving exceeds the typical inflow-to-outflow velocity ratio of in steady collisionless relativistic reconnection, i.e., the average rate at which reconnection can process incoming flux, potentially providing an additional source of variability. The lightcurves rise on -- light-crossing times of the reconnecting region, and the particle spectra develop power laws with index -- . These timescales are compatible with observed variability in high-energy sources, including the very-high-energy flares of M87 and the -ray flares of the Crab Nebula, making this model a viable framework for rapid flaring in active galactic nuclei and pulsar wind nebulae.

title: Generation of non-Maxwell-Boltzmann energy distributions during thermalization of interacting baths
abstract: We report on numerical experiments of thermalization between two reservoirs in which interspecies interactions are mediated via a Hamiltonian with a Gaussian dependence upon the distance between the particles. By using relatively high statistics, we are able to study deviations from the initially imprinted Maxwell-Boltzmann energy distributions as a function of the range and strength of the interaction, as well as the parameters of the two baths such as masses, trapping frequencies, that strongly affect the spatial overlap of the two species. At large interaction strengths and for any range, deviations are attributable to the sudden conversion of latent interaction energy into kinetic energy of the particles. In addition, long range interactions generate deviations even for interaction strengths in the weak regime, and non-uniform confinement introduces a further source of deviation from the Maxwell-Boltzmann energy distribution. This latter results in transient two temperature Maxwell-Boltzmann distributions suggestive of an inverse cascading route from inter-particle dynamics to thermalization. In the weakly-interacting regime, a simple expression for the equilibrium temperature is also obtained and discussed. These findings may be of relevance in the dynamics of exothermic chemical reactions, in the physics of ultracold atomic mixtures, and in self-sustained burning plasmas.

title: Dynamics of thermalization in classical three-dimensional many-body systems: Non-Maxwellian distributions and the role of anisotropic trapping
abstract: The physics of interacting baths is of interest in a variety of contexts, ranging from ultracold atoms to ionized gases. While many features can already be captured in a one-dimensional model, others are specific to the situation of two or three-dimensional systems. In this paper, we focus on three-dimensional features of a model for thermalization between two baths that we have explored in earlier publications. In contrast to the one-dimensional situation we show that, en route to thermalization, deviations from the Maxwell-Boltzmann energy distributions more akin to -distributions are observed. In three dimensions, these can be seen in changes at the peak of the distribution, which is precluded by the expected monotonic behavior of the energy distributions in one dimension. Furthermore, we consider thermalization for anisotropic trapping and explore its role in the onset of anomalous scaling with respect to the particle number. These results may be pertinent to the understanding of the interplay between turbulent behavior and nonlinearities for a variety of many-body classical systems.

title: Machine-learned spectral PDE solvers for fluids and plasmas
abstract: Sparse regression methods for discovering governing partial differential equations (PDEs) from data are sensitive to observation noise and are not constrained to reproduce the data under forward integration. We address both limitations by performing weak-form discovery in the spatial discretization in which the PDE is solved, learned by differentiating through multistep rollouts anchored at the observed states. The new method, Weak-form Anchored Rollout for PDEs (WARP), produces a machine-learned PDE solver. In this work, we focus on systems amenable to a spectral Galerkin solver. Across eight benchmark fluid and plasma systems, including high-dimensional turbulent simulations, WARP produces numerically stable rollouts from new random initial conditions and substantially improves coefficient recovery, rollout accuracy, and statistical measures compared with a single-step weak-form SINDy baseline.

title: Ion Heating in Pair-loaded Relativistic Turbulence
abstract: Pair-loaded relativistic turbulence is expected in compact high-energy astrophysical environments and may sustain plasma heating. Using self-consistent three-dimensional radiative particle-in-cell simulations, we identify the mechanism of ion heating mediated by pair-enhanced radiative feedback in relativistic turbulence. We derive the theoretical criterion for the transition to a regime dominated by radiative feedback and show that pair loading promotes the growth and persistence of large, connected optically thick structures. title: Vacancy and Helium-Cluster Thermomigration in Tungsten
abstract: Strong thermal gradients in tungsten plasma-facing components can bias the migration of irradiation-induced defects and thereby alter their redistribution, interaction, and retention. Here, we extend an atomistic jump-statistics framework previously developed for hydrogen to quantify the thermomigration of a single vacancy and interstitial He --He clusters in body-centered-cubic tungsten. Non-equilibrium molecular-dynamics simulations performed over several thermal gradients are used to determine the directional jump ratio, while geometrically derived projected jump lengths convert the fitted directional-bias coefficient into the heat-of-transport coefficient , where is the Boltzmann constant, the temperature, and a constant. All investigated defects exhibit negative values of , corresponding to net migration toward the hot region. He has the largest response, K , followed closely by the vacancy, whereas He exhibits the weakest response despite its intermediate cluster size. Independent constant-temperature simulations over 1000--1600 K show that He is also the least mobile cluster and has the largest effective migration energy, eV. In contrast, He is more mobile than He and has the smallest effective migration energy, 0.087 eV. Agreement between the He concentration profile predicted from the jump statistics and that obtained from a long molecular-dynamics trajectory provides an independent validation of the method. These results show that thermomigration cannot be inferred from cluster size, diffusivity, or migration energy alone and provide defect-specific heat-of-transport parameters for higher-length-scale models of tungsten under fusion-relevant thermal gradients.

title: Beyond Radiation Hydrodynamics: A Coupled Kinetic Plasma and Radiation Modeling of NIF Polar Direct Drive Capsule
abstract: Predictive modeling of inertial-confinement-fusion (ICF) implosions increasingly requires resolving ion-kinetic effects beyond the reach of radiation-hydrodynamics, without sacrificing radiation transport. We present, to our knowledge, the first coupling of a kinetic-ion plasma model to thermal radiation transport. The iFP code - a conservative, spherically symmetric, 1D2V hybrid kinetic-ion/fluid-electron Vlasov-Fokker-Planck solver - is extended with a grey P1 radiation model, coupled through a high-order/low-order (HOLO) fixed-point solver and advanced on a shared adaptive moving mesh. Opacities are mixed on the fly from the LANL TOPS library, exploiting the per-species information intrinsic to a kinetic code. We verify the implementation against the optically thick Marshak-wave and Mach-45 radiative-shock benchmarks, and apply it to a NIF polar-direct-drive exploding-pusher capsule. Increasing physics fidelity systematically improves agreement with the measured neutron yield and burn width; the improvement is driven by kinetically enhanced fuel leakage and ballistic preheating, and radiation transport proves essential for quantitative agreement. This work establishes a proof-of-principle capability for higher-fidelity kinetic-plasma/radiation modeling of ICF.

title: Correlated detection of electrons and ions emitted from laser-induced nanoplasmas in doped helium nanodroplets in the single-shot single-cluster regime
abstract: We present single-cluster single-shot correlated measurements of electron velocity-map images and ion time-of-flight traces from individual laser-induced nanoplasmas in xenon-doped helium nanodroplets. Simultaneous detection associates the ion composition, ion kinetic energies, and electron energies with the same nanoplasma event. The detected ion composition separates events into populations dominated by He+ mono-cations versus those dominated by He^{2+} di-cations, with markedly different ion energies and electron kinetic energies. The He+-dominated population correlates well with low electron kinetic energies (< 0.5 eV), whereas the distribution of maximum electron kinetic energies for the He^{2+}-dominated population shows a peak around 1 eV. Molecular dynamics simulations averaged over the focal volume suggest that local laser intensity contributes to this separation. These correlations provide single-event observables for classifying nanoplasmas and will support real-time shot-to-shot sorting in single-particle coherent diffractive imaging experiments.

title: Reinforcement Learning Controllers for Fusion Scenario Development
abstract: Scenario development, the design of the waveforms that take a tokamak discharge from breakdown to flat-top, is still an iterative, labour-intensive process. Every candidate scenario has to be simulated with a controller in the loop, and the classical shape and current controllers need low-level actuator references. So the process is iterative and includes a number of trial-and-error steps. We propose to replace the per-scenario controller tuning by a single goal-conditioned reinforcement-learning controller trained once, in advance, against a free-boundary equilibrium and transport simulator. A scenario is then specified only by the target waveforms of the physical quantities of interest (plasma current, line-averaged electron density, LCFS shape, x-point positions), and the controller produces the coil-current and fueling commands that realize them. We demonstrate the approach on an EAST plasma-current ramp-up: the controller takes over a small limited plasma, ramps the current and the density, grows the cross-section, forms two x-points and holds a double-null diverted configuration against sampled shape targets for the rest of a 1.2 s episode. The neural network controller is trained using TQC algorithm. On 1024 test scenarios sampled from a low-discrepancy scrambled Sobol sequence in 11-dimensional target space, the controller forms the divertor in 86% of the cases, holds it for more than 0.5 s in 67% and reaches the end of the episode in a diverted state in 58%, with flat-top tracking errors of a few kA in plasma current, m in density, cm in position and cm in x-point location; the failures concentrate at the high-current density ( ) region which is believed to be physically or from engineering perspective not feasible within ohmic mode.

title: Experimental verification of the PRIORA Monte Carlo code for proton radiography
abstract: PRIORA (Proton Radiography Ion-Optical Ray-tracing Analysis) is a fast Monte Carlo model for high-energy proton radiography. It combines fitted proton-matter interaction tables with energy-dependent transfer maps of arbitrary order and simulates approximately protons/s through a complete ion-optical system on an 8-core laptop. We verify it with GSI data obtained with the Ta_bench target: fifteen precision slits in a 2 mm Ta plate between symmetric PMMA staircases. A single experimental image provides the image scale, spatial resolution as a function of chromatic load, signed focus in both planes, effective angular acceptance and multiple-scattering contrast. With identical processing of experiment and simulation and no physics adjustment, PRIORA reproduces the data obtained with 2 and 4 GeV protons. At 2 GeV, PRIORA also recovers sub-percent quadrupole trims consistent with the control-system records and determines a target-plane spatial resolution of m.

title: Reduced Molecular Plasma Kinetics with Non-Boltzmann Vibrational Distribution
abstract: Vibrational kinetics can strongly affect energy transfer, chemical kinetics, and discharge behavior in molecular plasmas, but resolving all internal states is often impractical for reactor-scale simulation. Compact, physics-based vibrational closures are particularly needed when complete state-to-state (StS) data are limited. Starting from a detailed StS plasma-kinetics framework coupled to an electron-Boltzmann calculation, this work develops a reduced vibrational-kinetics formulation. The vibrational ladder is reduced to two non-Boltzmann groups that evolve their population and internal energy. State-resolved reaction rates and associated energy-exchange terms are projected onto the groups for subsequent tabulation in reactor-scale plasma models. StS-informed samples of the reduced-model are propagated for pulsed RF plasmas across a scan of pulse-averaged absorbed power and compared with the corresponding StS simulations. Predictions from the sampled models reproduce the bulk plasma response, including electron density, atomic-H density, and density. Discrepancies in production and the upper-energy-group vibrational temperature persist across the sampled reductions. This indicates a limitation of the present VDF reconstruction rather than the nominal parameter choice. Tail-sensitive processes therefore require a more accurate representation of the vibrational distribution.

title: Reconstruction of Unobserved Core Electron Density in Tokamak Plasmas with a Neural Operator Transport Surrogate and Uncertainty Quantification
abstract: Real-time control of tokamak plasmas requires the electron density profile. However, in a reactor-relevant device, diagnostic port access is limited and the profile can be observed only partially. In the present work we reconstruct the density profile by inferring the coefficients of a physics-based one-dimensional particle transport equation, using a Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) surrogate of the transport solver as a fast differentiable forward model. The surrogate enables realtime-compatible gradient-based reconstruction and uncertainty quantification from the reflectometry and interferometry measurements. We compare four uncertainty quantification methods - multi-seed ensembles, the Laplace approximation, Metropolis-Hastings, and a Gaussian method independent of the reconstruction fit. The resulting uncertainty is scored with CRPS and coverage calibration, separately on the observed and unobserved regions. We further demonstrate advantage of our approach over standard analytical function fit on synthetic and experimental DIII-D discharges.

title: Micrometer-thin liquid sheets from single-jet impact on a sharp edge for multi-kHz laser-plasma experiments
abstract: We present a simple and robust method for generating freely suspended liquid sheets by directing a single laminar liquid jet onto the sharp edge of an inclined plate. By optimizing liquid composition, impact geometry, and flow conditions, we identify a 60:40 ethylene-glycol-deionized-water volumetric mixture for stable sheet formation. The resulting sheets span 8 mm in height and 3 mm in width, with thicknesses from 1.1 to 4.8 micrometers measured by spatial and spectral interferometry. Operated in vacuum as continuously renewed plasma mirrors, these targets demonstrate stable performance from 0.5 to 10 kHz using 175-fs Yb:KGW laser pulses, reaching a maximum S-polarized reflectivity of 66.5% at an intensity of 4 x 10^14 W/cm^2. At higher intensities using 25-fs Ti:sapphire pulses at 1 kHz, maximum S-polarized reflectivity reaches 77% at 2 x 10^16 W/cm^2. The reflected beam exhibits high temporal stability, with angular pointing fluctuations of 18.19 +/- 0.53 microradians. Our results demonstrate a tunable, continuously renewed liquid-sheet target for multi-kHz laser-plasma experiments.

title: Critical magnetic Reynolds number of the weakly-collisional turbulent dynamo in supersonic plasmas
abstract: Weakly-collisional plasmas are found in several turbulent astrophysical environments, such as the Intra-galaxy-cluster medium (ICM) and the solar wind, where magnetic fields can be amplified by the turbulent dynamo. The onset of dynamo action is determined by the critical magnetic Reynolds number, , above which turbulent motions amplify magnetic energy. Although has been studied extensively in collisional magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) turbulence, its value in supersonic weakly-collisional plasmas remains unknown. Here we determine using three-dimensional hybrid particle-in-cell (HPIC) simulations of solenoidally driven turbulence with a sonic Mach number . We vary the magnetic Reynolds number over - and consider two initial plasma magnetisations, characterised by initial Larmor ratios and . We find that the magnetic energy grows exponentially at sufficiently large and decays when magnetic diffusion dominates at low . By fitting the magnetic-energy growth rate as a function of , we measure and for the initially magnetised and unmagnetised plasma, respectively. These values are the same within their uncertainties, indicating that the initial plasma magnetisation does not significantly affect in the supersonic regime. The measured values are higher than those previously obtained for the subsonic weakly-collisional dynamo, showing that increasing compressibility makes weakly-collisional turbulent dynamo action more difficult to excite. The measured values are also approximately 1.5 times higher than the value reported for supersonic MHD turbulence.

title: Intermittent turbulence as the driver of stochastic heating in the near-Sun solar wind
abstract: Understanding the mechanism by which the energy is dissipated at small scales to heat the outer corona and expanding solar wind, is a primary goal of the Parker Solar Probe (PSP) mission, and an outstanding question in heliophysics. Recent observational case studies have suggested that the dominant dissipation mechanism(s), stochastic heating (SH) or resonant heating (RH), may be modulated by the Alfvén `surface' ( ), while theoretical and simulation works predict that the mechanism should be modulated by the level of turbulence imbalance. We measure the local energy transfer (LET) rate from to solar radii from PSP observations, showing that the LET rate peaks at . We connect enhanced LET rates to signatures of intermittency, highlighting the key role that intermittent fluctuations play in heating the near-Sun solar wind. We compare the LET rate with estimates of the SH rate, finding that below solar radii the SH heating rate matches the LET rate provided intermittency is accounted for, regardless of , while farther from the Sun, SH is unable to account for the observed LET rate. In contrast to predictions by recent theoretical works, this implies that `imbalanced' intermittent stochastic heating may be a viable mechanism to heat highly imbalanced, low- collisionless plasmas, and is likely an important mechanism of dissipation in the outer solar corona and near-Sun solar wind.

title: ModeCast: One-Shot Prediction of Linear MHD Eigenmodes and Growth Rates in Tokamaks
abstract: Large-scale magnetohydrodynamic instabilities break plasma confinement, can trigger disruptions, and constrain fusion reactor design; modeling a single configuration against them takes hours with a reference solver such as JOREK, and a design study requires thousands of hours. ModeCast is the first learned surrogate to return the complete linear stability assessment for MHD modes. Trained on a comprehensive dataset of over 45,000 JOREK simulations across thousands of equilibria, it screens stability across toroidal mode numbers n=1-4 and predicts the full spatial structure and growth rate of unstable modes. Excluding the equilibrium solve, inference on a single GPU is over 10,000x faster than multi-core JOREK linear stability runs. The gain comes from building the linear-phase physics into the formulation, objective, and inputs, yielding up to six times more training data. ModeCast misses none of the unstable held-out cases, and its predicted fields reproduce the simulation's measured physics, from magnetic island topology to resistivity trends. On a fixed-geometry resistivity scan outside its training distribution, refitting only the 22k-parameter growth rate head of the 145M-parameter network on four simulation halves the held-out internal kink growth rate error, and fine-tuning the whole network adds little. Because it is differentiable and returns full fields, ModeCast could in the future assimilate experimental measurements, providing a bridge to real devices and accelerating progress toward commercial fusion. Project page: zenithon.ai/research/modecast.

title: Commutative Coarse-graining on the Sphere
abstract: Filtering by spatial convolution underlies coarse-graining and Large Eddy Simulation, the analysis of multiscale dynamics, and data processing across the sciences. Yet, as commonly practiced on the sphere, it violates a basic consistency requirement: commutation with differential operators, which is necessary for deriving coarse-grained dynamics and preserving the physics across lengthscales. We discuss the root of the problem, which is intrinsic to the curved geometry rather than being a result of metric terms, coordinate system, or numerical grid. A recently proposed generalized spherical convolution is, for a given scalar kernel, the unique linear operator commuting with the radial projection, divergence, and curl. Any consistent linear operator, be it spectral truncation, wavelet transform, diffusion, Green's-function inversion, or a machine-learned convolution, necessarily takes this form. From a simulation of an unstable jet, we demonstrate commutation to within numerical round-off, whereas common filtering that ignores curvature produces significant spurious divergence where none exists and gradient errors comparable to the gradients themselves.

title: Eulerian ion energisation in three-dimensional hybrid-Vlasov-Maxwell turbulence
abstract: In collisionless plasma turbulence, energy is transferred from electromagnetic fluctuations to the particles. However, the relative contributions of different ion energisation mechanisms remain unclear. We investigate ion energisation in three-dimensional hybrid Vlasov--Maxwell simulations of decaying turbulence at and , where is the initial ratio of ion thermal to magnetic pressure. Using the exact ion momentum equation, we decompose the ion energisation rate into the work done on the parallel, diamagnetic, curvature, agyrotropic and polarisation ion currents. This decomposition requires neither gyrotropy nor scale separation and, therefore, remains valid where guiding-centre theory breaks down. We show that the agyrotropic term, which has no guiding-centre counterpart, accounts for of the energisation at and at . We find that the dominant instantaneous energisation term changes with , from the polarisation current at low to the diamagnetic and agyrotropic currents at high , at all resolved scales. In addition, we show that reversible exchange with the ion bulk flow dominates the instantaneous rate, so the time-integrated energy transfer is larger at even though the instantaneous rate is smaller. Our results provide quantitative evidence that guiding-centre drifts alone cannot describe ion energisation in kinetic-scale turbulence and that the dominant energisation term depends on . The results also highlight the key role of non-local thermodynamic-equilibrium effects in energy conversion in collisionless plasma turbulence.

The results also highlight the key role of non-local thermodynamic-equilibrium effects in energy conversion in collisionless plasma turbulence.

title: Conservative Numerical Construction of Vlasov-Maxwell Equilibria and an Exact Cancellation of Flow by an Electrostatic Pressure-Gradient Flow
abstract: A class of Vlasov-Maxwell equilibria with pressure gradients is considered under symmetry assumptions that reduce the equilibrium equations to a nonlinear system of ordinary differential equations. Such equilibria provide self-consistent kinetic states with nonuniform thermodynamic profiles and potentially strong equilibrium electric fields, useful for fully kinetic stability studies of gradient-driven instabilities in the presence of equilibrium flows. The reduced equilibrium problem is posed as a nonlinear boundary-value problem for numerical solution, and a discretization is developed that preserves an associated energy invariant exactly at the discrete level. The resulting method provides a systematic means of computing nontrivial equilibria without relying on scale separation, and an alternative to constructing only approximately self-consistent initial states. A key property of the species flows, identified within this model for any distribution function of the constants of motion, is an exact cancellation between the flow and an electrostatically generated component of the pressure-gradient-driven flow. This follows directly from a structural property of the species force balance that arises from this type of symmetry reduction, and is verified numerically. Additional numerical results demonstrate the conservative properties of the discretization. Representative equilibrium configurations, relevant to future kinetic instability studies, are also presented. An asymptotic approximation for the interior equilibrium, derived in the well-magnetized, quasi-neutral regime, provides an independent check on these results. The present setting is deliberately simple, providing a controlled framework for constructing and analyzing self-consistent kinetic equilibria and a starting point for extensions to more general symmetry-reduced configurations.

title: Path-integrated electrostatic energization in laser-driven collisionless cylindrical convergence
abstract: Collisionless converging ion flows can sustain particle energization over an extended path, but the field channel responsible for the energy gain is not always identifiable. In laser-driven bladed microtube implosion, energetic carbon ions were previously observed alongside a self-generated gigagauss-class axial magnetic field [D. Pan and M. Murakami, Phys. Plasmas 32, 072107 (2025)], leaving the origin of their energization unresolved. Using two-dimensional particle-in-cell simulations, field-particle power decomposition and trajectory-resolved work accounting show that radial electrostatic work accumulated along the converging path supplies more than 98% of the net in-plane electric work, whereas the azimuthal channel associated with the time-varying magnetic field remains subdominant. The peak local mean ion energy factorizes, to good approximation, into an incident-flow contribution controlled by laser intensity and a geometric enhancement that grows approximately linearly with the inner radius because ions accumulate electrostatic work over a longer convergence path. The path-averaged radial electric field scales with the peak laser intensity as , favoring a geometry-pinned, comoving charge-separation structure over Debye-limited scaling. The peak local mean carbon-ion energy reaches 0.89 GeV. A smooth-cylinder control exhibits comparable peak energization, showing that blade modulation mainly affects poststagnation ion residence rather than the energy source.

title: Quantum Circuits for Variable-Coefficient Vlasov Dynamics via Schrödingerisation
abstract: High-dimensional Vlasov equations present promising use cases for quantum simulation, but their transport coefficients must be implemented coherently in order to preserve a compact quantum representation. We develop explicit Schrödingerised circuits for prescribed external field Vlasov dynamics without classical field updates. In 1D1V, velocity-dependent streaming is compiled directly from the encoded velocity register, while a non-linear cubic field is evaluated using reversible fixed-point arithmetic. For fixed polynomial degree, the field workspace scales linearly with the coordinate register width, while the field evaluation subroutine has polynomial depth. As a proof of concept, we simulate a minimal coupled 3D3V anharmonic Penning system and realise mixed electric-field terms and transverse magnetic coupling on a six-dimensional phase space in agreement with classical calculations. Resource analysis shows approximately linear growth with the number of time steps, while identifying the auxiliary register as the dominant depth bottleneck. Structured preparation and register recovery of the auxiliary state reveal an interplay between loading cost and readout. Together, our algorithm demonstrates a fully coherent quantum simulation of high-dimensional Vlasov dynamics with variable coefficients and identifies the practical resource costs that must be controlled for large-scale quantum implementation.

title: High average flux positron sources driven by a mJ-class laser
abstract: We report on the production and characterisation of MeV-scale positron populations driven by a high-repetition-rate, mJ-class laser system. The positrons are generated via a two-step Bethe--Heitler process driven by laser-wakefield-accelerated electron beams propagating through a mm-scale lead converter. At 10 Hz, approximately 1000 positrons in the 0.8--1.7 MeV energy range were measured over 100 accumulated shots. Stable electron acceleration was demonstrated at 10 Hz, 100 Hz, and 1 kHz using approximately 9 mJ of laser energy in the focal spot, indicating the potential for substantially higher average positron fluxes for laser systems operating at kHz repetition rates and energies of 10s of mJ. Such a positron source allows generating sufficiently high average fluxes of MeV-scale positrons while maintaining low positron yields per pulse and narrow temporal distributions, a regime of particular interest for novel applications in material science and fundamental physics. The measured positron yields and spectra are in good agreement with Monte Carlo simulations, supporting the modelling of the positron-production process and magnetic transport system.

title: Role of Device Size on Island Divertor Performance of W7-X-like Configurations
abstract: To examine how the island divertor performs in future low-shear stellarator reactors, we simulate (using EMC3-Eirene [1]) 3 different scales of W7-X: its current size, increased by a factor 2, and increased by a factor 4, where 4 times W7-X corresponds roughly to a reactor-scale device. For a single magnetic configuration, the standard magnetic configuration in W7-X, we examine how increasing the size of W7-X alters the divertor performance of the island divertor. We analyze how device scale shifts the location of the ionization source and the downstream density and temperature trends in the island divertor for achieving detachment. Local field line analysis shows that factor 2 and factor 4 size scalings achieve target densities via plasma ``self-baffling" within the open island divertor geometry. Finally, the heat and particle flux deposition on the scaled-up island divertor configurations are calculated. We observe a separation in the target heat and particle flux distribution with increased machine size in agreement with [2]. The target heat fluxes are at high separatrix densities. This shows that the separation of the heat and particle flux channels remains to be largely unproblematic. This analysis helps guide how to improve the open island divertor geometries for future stellarator reactors.

title: Properties and challenges of machine learning closures for ten-moment fluid models in the case of Landau damping
abstract: Two-fluid ten-moment models for plasma simulations evolve the velocity moments of the Velocity Distribution Function (VDF) up to the pressure tensor and require a closure for the divergence of the next velocity moment, the heat flux. We investigate the use of Machine Learning (ML) models for the discovery of heat flux closures, as an alternative to the typically employed Hammett-Perkins-like analytical closures. As a test case, we investigate Landau damping, which describes a resonant process of energy transfer between particles and waves. We find that fluid simulations with ML closures correctly reproduce both the damping frequency and the non-linear phase of Landau damping, and thereby outperform Hammett-Perkins-like closures, within the parameter ranges seen during training and when interpolating within those ranges. When extrapolating beyond the training data, the performance of the ML closure degrades with increasing distance from known parameters. We then investigate how well offline metrics (i.\,e.\; evaluating the trained model on fully-kinetic reference simulations, without inserting it into two-fluid simulations) can predict online performance, when the model is actually used in the two-fluid simulation. Our results show that offline metrics do not fully explain online performance, highlighting important implications for method evaluation in this field. We further investigate suitable metrics for online performance evaluation in the absence of a fully-kinetic reference simulation, which is often computationally expensive to run. We propose using the temporal evolution of entropy to evaluate the performance of reduced models with ML closures when no or few kinetic reference simulations are available.

title: Multiple Instance Learning for Interpretable Plasmoid Detection in the FLARE Device
abstract: Multiple instance learning (MIL) is a form of weakly supervised learning widely used in healthcare and biomedical imaging, where labels may be available for groups of observations ("bags") but not individual observations ("instances"). This setup is well-suited to plasmoid detection in magnetic reconnection experiments, since identifying dynamic magnetic structures is best accomplished taking in data from many time steps as a whole, as opposed to viewing frames in isolation. Instance-level consideration enables researchers to determine the range of times most affecting model output, thus serving as a tool for the temporal localization of plasmoids. Despite its success in the life sciences, to the best of our knowledge, MIL is yet to be reported in peer-reviewed plasma physics literature. We evaluate a MIL model against a convolutional recurrent neural network (CRNN), an architecture commonly found in plasma physics literature, on a plasmoid detection task, using a highly imbalanced dataset of 1152 magnetic reconnection shots from the FLARE device at PPPL. We demonstrate significant improvements in test performance (PR AUC: =+0.0932, p=0.0039; F1: =+0.0259, p=0.0488; Wilcoxon signed-rank test) against the CRNN model on full-channel input. We investigate the interpretability advantage provided by our MIL model for the temporal localization of plasmoids. Through its attention mechanism, we can discern relevant frames and even the number of plasmoids present in a shot. Overall, we show that MIL is a promising framework for similar event classification tasks in plasma physics.

title: Pair-exchange dynamics of magnetohydrodynamic turbulence
abstract: Nonlinear interactions in incompressible magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) and Navier-Stokes turbulence involve three spatial fluctuations conservatively exchanging, e.g., energy. The mathematical structure of a triad interaction does not allow to unambigously determine the specific contribution of each of the participating fluctuations to the resulting exchanges. Presently, only additional assumptions allow for the deconstruction of triad interactions into a sum of pair exchanges. This work proves that in incompressible MHD the simultaneous nonlinear transfer of cross-helicity sufficiently constrains the triad dynamics such that a mathematically unique pair-exchange representation of nonlinear energy and cross-helicity transfer is possible.

title: Sparking Dynamic, Relativistic Magnetic Reconnection in a Twisted Flux Tube
abstract: Magnetic reconnection around neutron stars (NSs) forms small-scale currents while transferring energy to electron-positron pairs. These dissipating currents cover a wide range of scales, potentially leaving an imprint on time-variable X-ray bursts and pulsed radio emission. We present a reduced, planar model of internal reconnection in a magnetic flux tube with relativistic magnetization, finite resistivity, and strong guide field. Comparing with realistic NS parameters, this model represents the dynamics of a slender magnetic flux tube that is much thinner than the stellar radius. The seed current profile is smooth and does not spontaneously reconnect; instead, a discrete and localized current perturbation is introduced, representing e.g. localized energy release from a NS crust or magnetosphere. Three high-resolution relativistic magnetohydrodynamics simulations are described: one has uniform resistivity and Lundquist number such that reconnection proceeds in the plasmoid-mediated regime; the other two account for the feedback of charge starvation on the resistivity in current layers, where density is depleted; we provide a more general explanation for this depletion. All simulations produce a few dominant magnetic X-points and a secondary Kelvin-Helmholtz instability that excites high-wavenumber currents. We quantify the reconnection rate, the intermittency of dissipation, and the time profile of current spikes. We further present three-dimensional simulations confirming a limited growth of the ideal kink mode in the strong guide field regime. Applications are discussed, including to radio pulse microstructure and current damping below the magnetar surface during an X-ray flare, leading to mass loss and X-ray afterglow.

title: Measuring electron density and electromagnetic fields in low-density laser-driven plasmas using proton radiography
abstract: In this paper, we describe a novel technique for inferring electron density in laser plasmas from proton-radiography data. Proton radiography is primarily a diagnostic for imaging electromagnetic field structures in such plasmas. In the presence of strong field gradients, `caustic' features arise and are broadened by the process of collisional scattering between the imaging protons and the plasma. This effect has a well defined density dependence, allowing for a robust measurement of electron number density. We validate the method on data from the turbulent-dynamo experiments performed at the Omega laser facility (with electron densities in the range of ), achieving good agreement with values obtained from Thomson scattering, x-ray imaging and simulations. This research enables one of the most robust techniques for measuring electromagnetic fields on laser-plasma experiments to simultaneously provide density measurements along the same line of sight, improving our ability to diagnose such plasmas.

title: Are regions essential for particle injection in relativistic magnetic reconnection?
abstract: During relativistic magnetic reconnection, X-points ( regions at vanishing guide field) have been proposed to play an essential role in injecting particles into the nonthermal population. Using fully kinetic particle-in-cell simulations at a range of magnetizations -- , we study in detail how the particle energy gains up to the injection threshold are partitioned into work done inside regions (unmagnetized), within one gyration after exit (re-magnetizing), and at all other times (magnetized). The magnetized channel supplies the largest part of the energy gain for of injected tracers at and at . Most of the tracers in this magnetized majority never enter an region before injection. We also compare these injection shares with the earlier studies that proposed an essential role for regions. We conclude that regions are neither necessary for injection nor the dominant direct contributors to pre-injection work by injection share in two-dimensional, nonradiative pair-plasma reconnection at vanishing guide field.

title: Quantitative validation of SMBI deposition profiles on EAST using experimentally constrained simulations
abstract: Quantitative comparison between SMBI fueling simulations and experiments has long been hampered by the poor constraint on the effective source. Here, the particle increment per pulse is extracted experimentally and used to calibrate the simulation source. For EAST shot 71438, the density evolution from microwave reflectometry is analyzed for nine SMBI pulse groups. The SMBI-induced density increase is isolated from the background by comparing the rising and falling phases around each pulse group. Its radial profile peaks in the mid-pedestal region for every pulse group. Volume integration of this increment provides the experimental reference. The simulations use a multi-fluid model in the BOUT++ framework in which two transport operators are recast into conservative flux form, with the particle balance residual reduced to about 2% of the injected amount, and the perpendicular transport coefficients are constructed from the discrete radial flux balance, with the unphysical changes of the initial density and temperature profiles in source-free evolution reduced by an order of magnitude. For three cases sharing the same nominal molecular flux, the simulated deposition peak agrees with the experimental one in the relative pedestal coordinate. The simulated conversion of the injected particles at the end of the injection is slightly lower than the value inferred from the experiment, while the fraction retained at the end of the pulse is higher. The perturbation thus decays more slowly in the simulation, which we attribute to fast loss channels not represented in the model, such as parallel losses to the scrape-off layer. The edge electron temperature stays on the high-temperature plateau of the dissociation and ionization rate coefficients throughout the pulse, and the inward shift of the deposition with edge cooling reported earlier does not occur under the present conditions.

title: Aluminum wide-range EOS sensitivity in Z-pinch dynamic-hohlraum liner-foam impact and outgoing radiation
abstract: In a Z-pinch dynamic hohlraum, an aluminum liner collides with a central foam and converts kinetic energy into radiation, and the liner-foam response depends on the aluminum equation of state (EOS). We construct a wide-range aluminum equation-of-state table from density functional theory (DFT) simulations over solid-liquid-plasma regions, denoted DFT-eos. Mixed deterministic-stochastic finite-temperature DFT (mDFT) gives the electron thermal contribution; quantum molecular dynamics (QMD) with classical calibration gives the ion part. We perform one-dimensional cylindrical radiation magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) simulations at a peak current of 50 MA and rise times of 220-300 ns on a single-layer light foam load. Opacity and electrical conductivity are fixed; only the liner Al EOS is changed between DFT-eos and the quotidian EOS (QEOS). Impact time and peak liner kinetic energy change little between the two tables. Larger differences appear in flight-segment density, the contact state at impact, and the time history of outgoing radiation power at the outer interface.

title: The impact of nonlinear Landau damping on cosmic ray streaming and the role of external turbulence
abstract: Cosmic rays (CRs) streaming faster than the Alfvén speed generate Alfvén waves that scatter them. The saturated wave amplitude is regulated by a damping mechanism. This damping controls the CR scattering rate and drift velocity, and thus the rate at which CRs transfer momentum and energy to the ambient plasma, which sets the strength of CR feedback. In the ionized interstellar medium, nonlinear Landau damping (NLLD) is commonly invoked as the dominant damping mechanism for Alfvén waves. We test this assumption with fluid-PIC simulations in which thermal ions and electrons are modeled as fluids with optional Landau closures, allowing us to compare otherwise identical runs with and without NLLD. When waves are self-generated by monoenergetic CRs, runs with and without Landau closures are indistinguishable: NLLD is inefficient and the CRs isotropize in the wave frame. Once high-amplitude Alfvén waves mimicking external turbulence are seeded, NLLD curbs wave growth and equalizes forward- and backward-propagating waves. We show that the saturated drift velocity, which falls below the Alfvén speed, can be accurately predicted from the wave spectra alone. If the CR distribution is undersampled, a numerical instability corrupts the largest resonant scales: unphysical, unresolved pitch-angle gradients resonantly generate backward-propagating waves, driving an inverse cascade that should be absent from purely streaming-driven waves. title: Flares and flux ropes: an entangled story
abstract: Solar flares serve as standard candles for all magnetic-reconnection-based energy releases, and their consequences into the heliosphere can be modeled from first principles. This review presents the latest developments in modeling solar flares and their associated flux rope expulsions with state-of-the-art multidimensional magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) descriptions. Observationally established ingredients beyond a single-fluid, thermal plasma evolution have been incorporated to varying degrees, and we highlight self-consistent efforts realized in "standard flare" setups.

title: Stationary Resistive MHD Solutions Near an Isolated Three-Dimensional Magnetic Null
abstract: Magnetic null points define the magnetic field topology in stellar coronae, planetary magnetospheres, and astrospheres, and are commonly associated with magnetic reconnection. We investigate the local structure of stationary three-dimensional (3D) resistive, incompressible magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) flows in the vicinity of an isolated magnetic null and an isolated velocity stagnation point, assuming that the two nulls are colocated. The governing MHD equations are solved self-consistently using a first-order local expansion of the magnetic and velocity fields about the null. For any given magnetic-null configuration, the equations admit a two-parameter family of stationary solutions, comprising multiple solution branches with distinct velocity topologies. Along these families, the velocity-null polarity can change at bifurcation points where the flow becomes effectively 2.5D. A single magnetic null can therefore support positive-radial, negative-radial, and spiral stagnation flows, with qualitatively different inflow, outflow, and rotational properties. The associated pressure and resistivity distributions are likewise determined self-consistently and vary across the solution family, demonstrating that they are coupled to the flow topology rather than prescribed independently. The generic solutions do not require the velocity and magnetic separatrices to coincide, allowing plasma to cross the magnetic fan separatrix and providing a local reconnective flow. These results demonstrate that, in the presence of nonuniform resistivity, the magnetic topology alone does not uniquely determine the associated stationary flow, pressure, or resistivity structure around a 3D magnetic null, revealing the nonlinear feedback between all macroscopic variables and resistivity. The constant-resistivity field-aligned and spiral field-crossing solutions identified previously are recovered as special cases.

title: Magnetic Reconnection Governs the Entire Lifecycle of Solar Eruptive Magnetic Flux Rope
abstract: While magnetic flux ropes (MFRs) are widely accepted to exist prior to many solar eruptions, the physical mechanism responsible for triggering and subsequently driving their eruptions remains debated. Classical models commonly attribute eruption onset to ideal magnetohydrodynamic instabilities, particularly the torus instability, while magnetic reconnection is often regarded as a secondary process. Using high-resolution three-dimensional MHD simulations, we investigate the eruption of an MFR that forms self-consistently through flux cancellation driven by converging motions and photospheric diffusion following an initial shearing phase. The pre-eruption MFR rises quasi-statically and reaches a height where the decay index exceeds the classical torus instability threshold, yet the system continues to evolve quasi-statically without eruption. Instead, eruption begins only when the current sheet beneath the MFR becomes sufficiently thin for magnetic reconnection to set in. Increasing numerical resolution systematically delays the eruption onset, whereas the decay index at eruption onset remains nearly unchanged, demonstrating that the onset is governed by reconnection rather than torus instability. During the eruption, magnetic reconnection continuously converts surrounding sheared arcades into newly reconnected twisted flux that merges with the pre-eruption MFR and continuously to build the erupting MFR. A component-resolved analysis of the Lorentz force work further shows that the newly reconnection flux contributes predominantly to the main acceleration phase. These results demonstrate that magnetic reconnection plays a central role throughout the entire lifecycle of the eruptive MFR: it builds the MFR, directly triggers its eruption, and provides the dominant driving of the eruption.

title: Coulomb collision operator
abstract: Properties of the Coulomb collision operator that have been found useful in plasma kinetic theory and plasma transport theory are gathered and reviewed, with derivations. The use of velocity-space coordinates appropriate to a magnetized (drift-kinetic) plasma is emphasized. Little of the material is new, although the derivations may be more detailed than is customary.

title: Controlling writhe in stellarator optimization
abstract: The writhe of a closed curve measures its coiling, and for a ribbon along it, writhe is the contribution to the linking number not due to twist. In stellarators, large writhe implies large helical excursion and has previously been either an uncontrolled outcome in optimization, or fixed beforehand by the choice of the coordinate system. We present a simple method to target the underlying writhe of the plasma boundary during optimization. Our method calculates writhe and linking number directly from the underlying elliptical boundary of the stellarator. It therefore does not require any properties of the MHD equilibrium solve, such as the true magnetic axis, making it fast to evaluate and smooth to differentiate. Examples for quasi-helically symmetric stellarators show that this target works well in practice.

title: Validation of geometric proxies using negative and positive triangularity plasmas with varying elongation on TCV and multi-machine gyrokinetic simulations
abstract: Negative Triangularity (NT) tokamak plasmas can achieve H-mode-like confinement while avoiding Edge Localized Modes, making them an attractive reactor scenario. Predicting in which configuration this benefit occurs requires understanding how magnetic geometry controls turbulent transport. Using a set of geometric proxies based on the poloidally averaged magnetic drift velocity, its poloidal variation, and Finite Larmor Radius (FLR) effects, this work validates their predictive power against gyrokinetic simulations and experiments. First, the proxies are used to predict how the relative benefit of NT over Positive Triangularity (PT) evolves with elongation , forecasting a detrimental effect of NT below -- . This prediction is confirmed by linear and nonlinear GENE simulations in both ITG- and TEM-dominated regimes. Additionally, a dedicated experimental elongation scan on TCV shows that NT plasmas at have and roughly 1.5 times larger than PT counterparts, while no difference is observed at . The analysis is then extended to realistic ITG-dominated scenarios from DIII-D, AUG, and JET, including up-down asymmetric equilibria where conventional triangularity-based descriptions break down. In all three devices, simulations of NT equilibria exhibit substantially reduced nonlinear heat fluxes relative to PT (factors of 1.8, 1.6, and 2.1, respectively). A systematic swap of geometric coefficients between NT and PT equilibria shows that magnetic drifts and FLR effects are the dominant stabilizing mechanisms across all machines, with parallel dynamics playing a secondary role. These results establish the geometric proxies as reliable, computationally inexpensive predictors of NT transport benefits across diverse shapes and turbulence regimes.

title: Effects of Coulomb Collisions on the Structures of Fast Magnetosonic Shocks
abstract: We present fully kinetic particle-in-cell simulations to demonstrate qualitative effects of binary Coulomb collisions on fast magnetosonic shocks. We find that with sufficiently high collisional frequencies, shock rippling and reformation can be inhibited, leading to stationary, laminar shock fronts. We observe that ion-ion collisions disrupt the motion of particles reflected back upstream that is the key for cyclical reformation. Meanwhile, the electron-ion collisions provide a Spitzer resistivity that can dissipate energy from the instability that causes shock rippling. This result helps us understand the role of collisions in laboratory shocks and possibly the outer heliosphere.

title: A modern particle-in-cell code for beam-beam simulations of future colliders
abstract: A key challenge in the design of next-generation colliders is predicting the effects of beam-beam interactions and using these predictions to optimize machine performance. Beam-beam interactions are characterized by strong focusing forces, radiative effects, and the generation of background particles. While analytical formulas provide insight into the dynamics of beam-beam interactions, these nonlinear, coupled effects are most accurately described with numerical methods. In this paper, we introduce the open-source particle-in-cell code WarpX as a modern tool for modeling the interaction point in future lepton colliders. WarpX provides high-performance execution on distributed GPU architectures within an open-source and actively maintained code base. We present convergence scans and benchmarks against the established beam-beam codes GUINEA-PIG (v1.2.2) and CAIN (v2.42) for luminosity spectra, photon emission, and secondary-particle production under a wide range of beam parameters corresponding to different collider concepts. Our results show that WarpX (v26.09) reproduces the benchmark beam-beam observables while enabling GPU-portable, extensible simulations. These results establish WarpX as a scalable platform for high-fidelity beam-beam modeling in future collider studies.

title: Dynamic Optimization Workflow for Gyrokinetic Stability and Transport
abstract: A dynamic optimization workflow for linear gyrokinetic stability that couples the gyrokinetic code CGYRO with the libEnsemble framework for ensemble management has been developed. The workflow is designed to efficiently explore multi-dimensional plasma parameter spaces and to address the practical challenges of simulation-driven optimization in fusion plasma physics, including expensive objective evaluations, unavailable gradient information, non-smoothness arising from transitions between dominant instability branches, and simultaneous multi-core simulations on high-performance computing resources. Rather than optimizing the growth rate at a single wavenumber, the objective maximizes the growth rate-to-wavenumber ratio over the ion-scale spectrum. A derivative-free, model-based optimization algorithm employs manifold sampling to handle the nonsmooth composite structure of the objective function. The approach is applied to the optimization of local magnetic flux-surface shaping parameters, with an equilibrium baseline drawn from DIII-D negative triangularity experimental parameters. The workflow is general and extensible and provides a foundation for future optimization studies involving nonlinear transport objectives and higher-dimensional parameter spaces.

title: QUARZ: a quasi-static particle-in-cell code with non-uniform radial grids for plasma wakefields
abstract: We present a quasi-static particle-in-cell scheme for beam-driven plasma wakefields in cylindrical geometry that works on an arbitrary non-uniform radial grid. The field equations are discretized with hat-function finite elements and conservative finite volumes on any monotone set of radial nodes, and the transverse magnetic field is obtained explicitly, without iterations, following Baxevanis and Stupakov. An optional azimuthal mode describes beam offsets, tilts and hosing. The discretization keeps the discrete Gauss law exact, deposits a uniform plasma exactly on every node including the axis, and remains second-order accurate on smoothly stretched grids. Resolution can therefore be placed where the physics needs it. For a tightly focused witness beam that pulls the plasma ions onto the axis, a grid that is fine only near the axis gives the same near-axis fields as a uniform grid with the same axis resolution, with thirty times fewer cells and in thirty times less computing time. Such a grid also resolves the singular closure of a cold-plasma bubble, which a uniform grid hides by smoothing it over one cell; smoothing the plasma sources over a fixed length, chosen independently of the grid, regularizes the closure and makes the wake behind it converge. The scheme is implemented in the open-source C++/Kokkos code QUARZ (Quasistatic Arbitrary-resolution RZ), which runs on CPUs and GPUs and uses MPI with a pipelined decomposition along the co-moving coordinate. Simulations of the self-modulation of the AWAKE proton bunch agree with the three-dimensional code HiPACE++. QUARZ is, to our knowledge, the first production-grade simulation code in plasma physics that is \emph{zero-touch}: all of its source code, tests and documentation were written by an AI agent directed by a physicist who did not write a single line of the code.

title: Relativistic Six-Fluid Rotating-Plasma Force-Balance Equilibria for p-11B Fusion Conditions in Spherical Tori
abstract: We formulate an axisymmetric spherical torus (ST) six-component magnetofluid equilibrium model for p_11B plasmas composed of thermal and suprathermal proton, boron, and electron fluids. The model is designed for p_11B parameter regimes where ion energies, strong current drive, energetic electron populations, and ion-electron temperature separation can render a single_fluid static_equilibrium description inadequate. It generalizes rotating_plasma equilibrium theory by incorporating relativistic thermal enthalpy corrections to the electron fluids via h(T/m_ec^2) and by constructing modified flux functions Y_α associated with canonical angular momentum for each component α. The equilibrium is determined by a Grad-Shafranov-like Ampere law for the poloidal magnetic flux Psi, algebraic density relations constrained by quasineutrality, and prescribed profile functions F_α(Y_α), T_α(Y_α) and K_α(Y_α). The manuscript includes the relativistic magnetofluid equations, the axisymmetric equilibrium formulation, the six_fluid computational method, and four numerical equilibria: two reactor_relevant ST p_11B parameter sets and two EHL-2 ST cases. The examples span toroidal beta b_T = 0.058_0.253, plasma currents I_p = 2.697_12.59 MA, and suprathermal electron temperatures T_eh = 287 keV_2.37 MeV, with h up to 19.1. Over these parameter ranges, Ampere's law accuracy, electrostatic potential accuracy, and component_resolved radial force balance can have errors ranging from 3% to below 0.1%. These results indicate that high-temperature p_11B ST equilibria can differ qualitatively from the single_fluid tokamak equilibria and require analysis of equilibrium component_resolved force balance, relativistic electron enthalpy, and explicit reproducibility diagnostics.

title: Implicit PIC Simulations of Hydrogen Plasmas with Intense Negative Ion Production
abstract: High-density plasma discharges in hydrogen operating at low pressures are of considerable interest for negative ion production used in many applications. Their weak collisionality requires a kinetic, nonlocal description, and a popular approach is to model such discharges numerically using the particle-in-cell (PIC) method combined with Monte Carlo collisions (MCC). However, the most commonly used explicit momentumconserving variant of this method is highly inefficient because it must resolve both the Debye length and the plasma period. In this context, the implicit energy-conserving PIC/MCC scheme appears to be an attractive alternative, as it can model the plasmas of interest using their actual parameters without resorting to artificial scaling techniques. This work considers simulations of two types of high-density plasma discharges performed using electromagnetic or electrostatic energy-conserving PIC/MCC codes in hydrogen, and discusses the observed negative ion production.

title: Radial increase of the compensated interplanetary magnetic field magnitude as a result of the growth of spherically polarized Alfvén waves
abstract: Measurements from the NASA Parker Solar Probe (PSP) mission demonstrate that inside solar radii ( ) the magnitude of the interplanetary magnetic field does not fall off simply as , with 15--20\% below its value at . Here we use PSP magnetic field measurements over -- to show that the outward rise of is not due to the global structure of the heliospheric magnetic field or proximity to the heliospheric current sheet but is the direct result of the growth of large-amplitude, spherically polarized Alfvén waves (so-called `switchbacks'). Over the same distance range, stays constant, so that the sector-signed radial flux is conserved. The wave amplitude grows from to as , and rises by . A simple model parametrized by the broadening of the distribution of deflection angles reproduces the effect to high accuracy. These results demonstrate that as the relative wave amplitudes grow with increasing solar distance, a dynamo-like process operates to enhance the field magnitude by up to . By enhancing magnetic pressure this has implications for the large scale solar wind structure in the low-beta inner heliosphere, as well as partially resolving the long-standing discrepancy between remote measurements of the solar magnetic field and those made in situ by earlier missions farther from the Sun.

title: A reduced model for neoclassical transport in non-axisymmetric magnetic configurations
abstract: A unified framework is proposed to compute a neoclassical equilibrium for tokamaks with non-axisymmetric magnetic perturbations, based on a Hamiltonian description combined with a variational approach that relies on a principle of minimum entropy production. This approach allows for a transparent identification of the respective contributions from different classes of trapped particles in magnetic well minima. Analytic expressions are derived for specific collisionality regimes, and a fast and efficient numerical procedure is devised to compute the entropy production rate. Finding the extremum of the entropy production leads to tractable expressions of transport coefficients that can be computed quickly and efficiently.

title: Plasma-neutral collision operators for hydrogen isotopes: kinetic and gyrokinetic descriptions, comparison to fluid
abstract: Plasma-neutral interactions critically affect the edge dynamics of magnetically confined fusion devices. Neutral atoms modify ion and electron velocity distributions, potentially affecting local instabilities Standard fluid models simplify these processes (namely charge exchange, ionization and recombination) using Maxwellian assumptions and linearized source terms. We revisit these assumptions for a hydrogen plasma interacting with hydrogen atoms. We derive plasma-neutral interaction terms in the kinetic and gyrokinetic frameworks. Accounting for velocity-dependent differential cross-sections, the model captures the kinetic impact of inelastic collisions on ions and electrons beyond energy and momentum exchange. We demonstrate that the fluid moments of the kinetic model reduce to standard fluid source terms under the appropriate assumptions of Maxwellianity and linearity. We compare the kinetic model with fluid models through their effects on distribution functions and fluid moments. Substantial discrepancies are observed, even for Maxwellian distributions. For charge exchange, the kinetic model yields momentum and energy exchange rates up to twice those predicted by fluid descriptions. We show that a fluid treatment of ionization greatly overestimates the mean kinetic energy of the produced electrons. These results highlight the limitations of fluid descriptions and the importance of kinetic effects in edge-plasma momentum and energy exchange.

title: Toward a Multimodal Foundation Model for Plasma State Reconstruction
abstract: Plasma experiments observe coupled physical states through sparse, heterogeneous, and incomplete diagnostics. We present a proof of concept toward a multimodal foundation model for plasma state reconstruction during magnetic reconnection, motivated by the Facility for Laboratory Reconnection Experiments (FLARE). Using 250 synthetic VPIC simulations at fixed reference electron beta , with 225 training runs and 25 disjoint validation runs, we train a 5.5M-parameter residual 3D U-Net to reconstruct three magnetic-field components and electron density from incomplete observations. The model combines spatial-only pooling, which preserves all 24 temporal frames, with global spatiotemporal self-attention and rotary positional encoding. Independently masking magnetic and density modalities across random, grid, block, and temporal patterns enables sparse sensing, cross-modal completion, density super-resolution, and temporal completion with a single set of weights and no task-specific retraining. With density fully hidden, just 0.1% magnetic spatial visibility reduces median density NRMSE from approximately 0.9 to 0.1. Conversely, observed density improves current-density reconstruction when magnetic data are absent or extremely sparse. With no magnetic observations, roughly 1% density visibility approaches the density reconstruction accuracy achieved with fully observed magnetic fields, although current structure remains more dependent on direct magnetic measurements. Full magnetic conditioning also stabilizes completion of missing future density frames. These results demonstrate bidirectional cross-modal predictive coupling within this simulation regime. Generalization across plasma regimes or to experimental measurements remains untested.

title: Multi-Objective Design of C-Shaped Targets for Energy--Divergence Control in Laser-Driven Proton Acceleration
abstract: We optimize the energy-divergence trade-off of laser-driven protons from a C-shaped target using two-dimensional particle-in-cell simulations and constrained multi-objective Bayesian optimization. Five geometry and focusing parameters are varied to maximize proton cutoff energy and minimize the RMS divergence of forward protons with E_k >= 5 MeV under a proton-only conversion-efficiency constraint of eta_H >= 9%. Of 82 designs, 60 are feasible and 15 Pareto-optimal. The Max-Energy and Min-Divergence endpoints yield 28.64 MeV at 52.51 degrees and 11.47 MeV at 11.13 degrees, respectively; a representative compromise yields 21.44 MeV at 38.44 degrees. Matched-stage diagnostics link these regimes to optical-field buildup, electron energization, charge separation, and outer-sheath organization. Numerical tests support the principal trends. Reflection timing does not support a monotonic trapping-duration law, and the charge-sheath relation remains non-local. These results establish a design-resolved route to controlling proton energy and angular quality.

title: First achievement of 100 million degree electron temperatures in a spherical torus: the EXL-50U
abstract: Here,we report an ST plasma in which Thomson scattering measures a central electron temperature exceeding 8.6 keV (100 million degrees kelvin) on the EXL-50U spherical torus device.The high-temperature phase is obtained at low density by sequential operation of two 50 GHz ECRH systems: ordinary-mode (O-mode) ECRH3 followed by extraordinary-mode (X-mode) ECRH4. In contrast to neutral-beam-heated high-ion-temperature ST scenarios, the discharge is sustained by ECRH only.

title: SPIRE: Spin-Resolved Particle-in-Cell with Radiative Corrections for Extreme Laser--Plasma Interactions
abstract: We present SPIRE, a spin- and photon-polarization-resolved particle-in-cell (PIC) code for self-consistent simulations of laser-plasma interactions in the strong-field quantum electrodynamics (QED) regime. The classical PIC framework combines a Yee-grid finite-difference time-domain Maxwell solver, a relativistic Boris particle pusher, shape-function particle-grid interpolation, Esirkepov charge-conserving current deposition, laser boundary injection, and a relativistic moving window in one, two, and three spatial dimensions. A vectorial Laguerre-Gaussian laser injector based on an angular-spectrum formulation supports tightly focused, nonparaxial optical orbital-angular-momentum modes. The strong-field QED module treats nonlinear Compton scattering and nonlinear Breit-Wheeler pair production as stochastic processes using spin- and polarization-resolved probabilities in the local constant-field approximation. Electron and positron spin evolution includes stochastic transitions, no-emission corrections, and Thomas-Bargmann-Michel-Telegdi precession with a field-dependent anomalous magnetic moment. Photon polarization is represented by the Stokes vector and evolves through nonlinear Compton scattering, pair production, vacuum birefringence, and vacuum dichroism. The implementation is verified with one-, two-, and three-dimensional benchmarks. Classical PIC results are cross-checked against SMILEI, and the spin- and polarization-resolved QED modules reproduce published results for polarized electron generation, vacuum birefringence and dichroism, and dense polarized positron production. These benchmarks verify the coupled classical PIC, strong-field QED, spin, and photon-polarization modules implemented in SPIRE.

title: A New Degree of Freedom in Stellarator Coil Design
abstract: Reversed toroidal field (RTF) coils introduce a new degree of freedom in stellarator coil design. While the total plasma-linked current is fixed by Ampere's law, compensating RTF currents allow the modular-coil current to exceed this value without altering the net linkage. This redistribution decouples key coil constraints and modifies the external coil geometry without significantly compromising the confining magnetic field. As a result, the achievable coil-plasma separation can be increased in the configurations studied, potentially enabling more compact stellarator designs.
